props.title: Ridicule
props.initialSlug: Wit is the weapon in the court of Versailles.

sections.content: Ridicule (1996) masterfully captures the lethal power of wit in pre-Revolutionary France, where a sharp tongue could make or break social standing. Director Patrice Leconte crafts a devastating portrait of Versailles' cruel verbal combat, where wordplay becomes weaponry. Like Dangerous Liaisons (1988) and Amadeus (1984), the film exposes how aristocratic games masked deeper societal rot. Charles Berling plays Ponceludon, a provincial nobleman seeking funds for swamp drainage, forced to navigate a court where clever insults matter more than actual deeds.

sections.content: The film's brilliant screenplay by Rémi Waterhouse uses language as both entertainment and weapon. Every verbal duel carries lethal stakes, recalling the intellectual sparring in The Last Duel (2021) or Barry Lyndon (1975). The court scenes crackle with tension as reputations rise and fall on a single bon mot. Fanny Ardant delivers a masterclass as the calculating Madame de Blayac, whose wit masks ruthless ambition.

Beyond its razor-sharp dialogue, Ridicule offers a scathing critique of aristocratic decadence. Like Marie Antoinette (2006) and The Death of Louis XIV (2016), it shows a ruling class fiddling while France burns. The contrast between Versailles' glittering word games and the provinces' deadly swamps highlights the moral bankruptcy that would spark revolution. sections.content: The film's attention to period detail rivals Jefferson in Paris (1995) and A Tale of Two Cities (1989), but with a sharper political edge. Every powdered wig and ornate costume underscores the grotesque inequality of the era. The script's wit serves a deeper purpose - exposing how language became a tool of class warfare, keeping outsiders at bay while protecting elite privilege.
